title: The Itinerarium: the Mount of God, the Calendar of Jerusalem, and the Road to Edessa
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Shore of the Western Ocean

stops.name: Gallaecia, the coast that may not be hers
stops.date_confidence: placeholder only. No source gives Egeria's birth year, decade, parents, or town; the year 350 is a bare convenience for ordering, not a claim.
stops.campa: Nothing in her own hand says where she began. The manuscript's first leaves are gone, and with them the outward road and whatever she wrote of home. Three centuries later a monk of the Bierzo tells his brothers she was sprung from the farthest shore of the western sea, the Ocean, and on that one clause Marius Ferotin builds the Iberian case in 1903. A coastline stands in for a birthplace. No contemporary source names her house, her family, or her rank, and none ever did in any copy that survived.
stops.quote: extremo occidui maris Oceani littore exorta
stops.quote_source: Valerius of Bierzo, Epistola ad fratres, quoted in McClure and Feltoe (trans.), The Pilgrimage of Etheria (1919), p. viii
suggested_refs: The Galician Atlantic coast, the 'shore of the western Ocean' of Valerius's letter
sources: Valerius of Bierzo, Epistola ad fratres (c. 680)
Marius Ferotin (1903)
Wikipedia, 'Egeria (pilgrim)'
Hagith Sivan, 'Who Was Egeria?', HTR 81 (1988)

stops.name: Narbonne, the rival homeland
stops.date_confidence: not a recorded stop. This pin marks a scholarly hypothesis about her origin, placed here for the contradiction it holds against the Galician pin, not for any journey Egeria is known to have made.
stops.campa: Karl Meister reads the same Latin in 1909 and finds no Iberian sound in it at all. He notes her comparison of the Euphrates to the Rhone and puts her instead in a religious house of Gallia Narbonensis, in southern Gaul. The two proposals do not reconcile: Valerius points to Spain, the philology points to Gaul, and no manuscript decides between them. Mary Magdalene's legend lands her on this same Gallic shore at Saintes-Maries-de-la-Mer three and a half centuries earlier, on evidence no firmer.
suggested_refs: Karl Meister's 1909 philological argument against the Gallaecian attribution
sources: Karl Meister (1909), cited in Wikipedia, 'Egeria (pilgrim)'
Encyclopedia.com, 'Egeria, Itinerarium of'

stops.name: Faran, thirty five miles short of the mountain
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed. Egeria gives the distance from the mount of God, not a date; the December 382 placement follows Devos's 381-384 frame and the Epiphany she keeps in Egypt three weeks later.
stops.campa: Thirty five miles short of the mount of God, in a valley fed by a spring, the party rests two days at Faran before the climb. Egeria gives the oasis no relic and no miracle, only its distance and its use. She does not call it a bishopric: the see of Pharan is founded later, in 451, to govern the monks of the peninsula. The party rides out again with the spring at its back and thirty five miles of open desert lying between them and the mountain of God.
suggested_refs: The Wadi Feiran oasis, principal watering station of the Sinai crossing
sources: Egeria, Itinerarium ch. 1, trans. McClure and Feltoe (CCEL)
Wikipedia, 'Pharan (Sinai)'

stops.name: The plain beneath Sinai, where the camp is shown
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed from the Devos chronology; Egeria dates none of the Sinai stops.
stops.campa: The plain beneath the mountain runs sixteen miles long and four miles broad by her measure, and here, she is told, all Israel camped through the forty days Moses spent above. Guides point out the ground where the golden calf was cast, a great stone over the graves of those who craved meat, and the outlines of tents still legible in the dirt. She writes down what is shown to her without ruling on it. Moses crossed this valley in the atlas thirteen centuries before her donkeys reach it.
stops.quote: And across the valley appeared Sinai, the holy mountain of God.
stops.quote_source: Egeria, Itinerarium, 'The Approach to Sinai,' trans. McClure and Feltoe, The Pilgrimage of Etheria (1919), p. 1
suggested_refs: The plain of er-Raha, northwest of the later monastery, traditional site of the Israelite camp
sources: Egeria, Itinerarium ch. 2 and 5, trans. McClure and Feltoe (CCEL)
moses.journey.json

stops.name: Mount Sinai, the ascent as if up a wall
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed. The surviving text opens mid-sentence on this approach and carries no date at all; only the sabbath arrival is given.
stops.campa: They reach the mountain late on the sabbath and sleep at the monastery in the valley; the ascent begins before dawn. The path goes straight up the whole way, as if up a wall, and the party climbs it on foot. At the summit stand a small church and a priest who lives there, and the monks show her the cave where Moses received the second tablets. She takes communion at the top. Nothing grows on the peak, she writes, no scrub and no grass, bare rock down to the ground.
stops.quote: We reached the mountain late on the sabbath, and arriving at a certain monastery, the monks who dwelt there received us very kindly.
stops.quote_source: Egeria, Itinerarium, trans. McClure and Feltoe, The Pilgrimage of Etheria (1919), p. 3
suggested_refs: The summit church of Jebel Musa, standing in the 380s, long before Justinian's works
sources: Egeria, Itinerarium ch. 1-3, trans. McClure and Feltoe (CCEL)
moses.journey.json

stops.name: Horeb, the cave of Elijah
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the text gives sequence, not dates.
stops.campa: On the neighbouring summit the monks show her the cave where Elijah hid from Jezebel, and beside it the stone altar the prophet is said to have raised, with a church built over the place. Sinai and Horeb are two names carried by two peaks of one massif, which is the local monks' geography and not a surveyed distinction; scripture itself uses the names interchangeably and never divides them across a ridge. Egeria takes the arrangement down as the monks give it to her.
suggested_refs: The chapel of Elijah on the saddle below the summit of Jebel Musa
sources: Egeria, Itinerarium ch. 4, trans. McClure and Feltoe (CCEL)

stops.name: The Burning Bush, alive and putting out shoots
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; undated in the text.
stops.campa: At the head of the valley, inside a walled garden with abundant water, she is shown the bush from which God spoke to Moses. It is alive, she writes, and still putting out shoots. Monks' cells stand around the garden and the party prays there. No fortress encloses the ground yet: Justinian's walls are a hundred and seventy years off, and the monastery that will carry Catherine of Alexandria's name is raised here in the next century. Antony of Egypt's discipline already shapes the men she meets.
suggested_refs: The walled garden of the Burning Bush, later enclosed within Saint Catherine's Monastery
sources: Egeria, Itinerarium ch. 4, trans. McClure and Feltoe (CCEL)
san_antonio_abad.journey.json
catherine_alexandria.journey.json

stops.name: Clysma, the port at the head of the Red Sea
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed from the return sequence; undated in the text.
stops.campa: The road back from Sinai runs north to Clysma, the port at the head of the Red Sea and the Suez of later maps, where the grain ships and the pilgrim traffic meet. Egeria gives it no shrine and no story. She names it once and moves inland. It is a station, one link in the chain that carries her from the bare rock of the peninsula to the wet fields of the delta. Her text spends pages on any ground that holds scripture and a single line on a harbour that only holds ships.
suggested_refs: The Roman harbour of Clysma at the head of the Gulf of Suez
sources: Egeria, Itinerarium ch. 7, trans. McClure and Feltoe (CCEL)

segments.name: Egypt, and the Roads of the Exodus

stops.name: The land of Goshen, crossed in two days
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed. Egeria gives two days of travel and the Epiphany that follows, not a calendar date for the crossing.
stops.campa: She crosses the land of Goshen, the territory scripture assigns to Jacob's family in Egypt, treating it as a named country rather than a single site and taking two days over it. The Exodus is a map she can walk, laid over roads that Roman Egypt actually maintains. Northwest, in Alexandria, Hypatia will open her school within a decade of this crossing, teaching geometry in a city whose Christians and pagans are already circling one another. Egeria passes through and mentions none of it.
suggested_refs: The Wadi Tumilat and eastern Delta, the conventional extent of biblical Goshen
sources: Egeria, Itinerarium ch. 7-9, trans. McClure and Feltoe (CCEL)
hypatia.journey.json

stops.name: The city of Arabia, Epiphany with a bishop she already knew
stops.date_confidence: the feast is fixed at 6 January by her own account; the year is reconstructed within the 381-384 frame.
stops.campa: Epiphany finds her at the city of Arabia, inside Goshen, where the bishop keeps her two days. She calls him a holy man and truly a man of God, and adds the detail that fixes him: he was already known to her from the time she had been in the Thebaid. That remark is the only surviving trace of an Egyptian journey the manuscript otherwise loses. Her pilgrimage is a calendar as much as a route: Epiphany is kept where the road has put her, in a delta town whose bishop she first met somewhere else entirely.
suggested_refs: Phacusa, modern Faqus, generally identified with Egeria's 'city of Arabia'
sources: Egeria, Itinerarium ch. 9, trans. McClure and Feltoe (CCEL)

stops.name: Rameses, open country and ruins in great numbers
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed from the sequence; Egeria gives the distance from the city of Arabia, four miles, and no date.
stops.campa: Four miles from the city of Arabia she stands in the ruins of Rameses and finds open country without a single habitation, though ruins in great numbers. A great stone brought from Thebes carries two carved figures the guides call Moses and Aaron; an old sycamore is named the tree of truth. The delta capital under her feet is the Pi-Ramesses of the Egyptian records, near modern Qantir. She counts the ruins and repeats the names her guides give the stone and the tree, without testing either.
suggested_refs: Pi-Ramesses at Qantir, the delta capital whose ruins Egeria walked
sources: Egeria, Itinerarium ch. 8-9, trans. McClure and Feltoe (CCEL)

stops.name: Tatnis, once Pharaoh's metropolis
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed from the sequence; undated in the text.
stops.campa: Two days across Goshen bring her to Tatnis, which she is told was once Pharaoh's own capital and is the city where holy Moses was born. She reports the claim as her hosts give it and attaches no authority to it beyond them. Scholars since have proposed the equation with Tanis, San el-Hagar in the eastern delta; no inscription confirms it and it remains a proposal. Scripture names no city for the birth of Moses at all, and the delta has supplied one for the pilgrims who come asking.
suggested_refs: Tanis, San el-Hagar, the reconstructed identification of Egeria's Tathnis
sources: Egeria, Itinerarium ch. 9, trans. McClure and Feltoe (CCEL)

segments.name: The Holy City, Day by Day

stops.name: The Anastasis, the office before cockcrow
stops.date_confidence: the daily office has no single date. This pin stands for a routine she describes as unvarying across the year; the February 383 stamp is an ordering convenience.
stops.campa: Every day of the year the doors of the Anastasis open before cockcrow, and monks and virgins keep vigil inside the rotunda raised over the tomb. At dawn the people come; at the sixth hour, the ninth, and again at lucernare, the city gathers. Candles are lit from a lamp burning inside the cave itself. The bishop enters the rock and blesses those waiting at the rail. Egeria writes it down hour by hour, and hers is the earliest eyewitness record of how this church was used.
suggested_refs: The rotunda of the Anastasis over the tomb, in its Constantinian form
sources: Egeria, Itinerarium ch. 24, trans. McClure and Feltoe (CCEL)
jesus.journey.json

stops.name: The Martyrium, the greater church Constantine built
stops.date_confidence: no date in the text; the Sunday liturgy she describes is a weekly routine, stamped here for ordering.
stops.campa: Behind the rock of Golgotha stands the greater church, decorated, she writes, with gold and mosaic and costly marbles in the nave and in the sanctuary alike. Constantine had the temple of Venus pulled down for it in 326 and Bishop Macarius raised the basilica; fifty seven years later Egeria watches the whole city assemble in it before dawn on Sundays, every priest who wishes preaching in turn and the bishop closing. His masonry and her sentences are two halves of one record.
suggested_refs: The Martyrium basilica on Golgotha, demolished temple of Venus beneath it
sources: Egeria, Itinerarium ch. 25, trans. McClure and Feltoe (CCEL)
constantino_el_grande.journey.json

stops.name: Jerusalem, the eight weeks of Lent
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed. Egeria describes the Lenten cycle without naming a year; the 383 stamp follows the Devos frame.
stops.campa: She measures Jerusalem's Lent against the Lent she knows at home and finds it strange. Here the fast runs eight weeks, not forty days, because neither the Lord's Day nor the sabbath is a fast day; deduct the eight and the seven and forty one fast days remain. Among the ascetics she calls apotactitae the discipline is harder: no bread that can be weighed, no oil, nothing that grows on a tree, only water and a little gruel of flour. The count is hers, worked out on the page for sisters at home who fast on a different reckoning.
stops.quote: Just as with us forty days are kept before Easter, so here eight weeks are kept before Easter.
stops.quote_source: Egeria, Itinerarium, trans. McClure and Feltoe, The Pilgrimage of Etheria (1919), p. 57
suggested_refs: The Jerusalem eight-week Lent, distinct from the western forty days
sources: Egeria, Itinerarium, Lent section, trans. McClure and Feltoe (1919), p. 57

stops.name: Jerusalem, the liturgy in three languages
stops.date_confidence: no date given; the arrangement she describes is continuous, and the stamp is for ordering only.
stops.campa: The bishop of Jerusalem knows Syriac and preaches in Greek regardless, and a priest stands beside him turning every sentence into Syriac so that the congregation follows. Behind them a third relay works for the Latins, who have neither language, translated by brothers and sisters who hold both. Egeria is writing for sisters at home who read Latin. She is describing, from inside it, the machinery that lets a woman from the western ocean stand in a Greek liturgy in a Syriac city and follow it.
stops.quote: there is always a priest standing by who, when the bishop speaks Greek, interprets into Syriac, that all may understand what is being taught
stops.quote_source: Egeria, Itinerarium, trans. McClure and Feltoe, The Pilgrimage of Etheria (1919), p. 94
suggested_refs: The trilingual catechetical practice of 4th-century Jerusalem
sources: Egeria, Itinerarium, catechesis section, trans. McClure and Feltoe (1919), p. 94

stops.name: Sion, the reading where the reading happened
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed. Pentecost 383 fell in late May by the Julian reckoning; Egeria supplies the feast, not the date.
stops.campa: On Wednesdays and Fridays through Lent, and at the ninth hour on ordinary days, the community climbs to Sion, the hill that holds the room of the Last Supper and the descent of the Spirit. At Pentecost the reading from Acts is timed to fall in the place where scripture puts the event. The building she describes stands under the ground of the later Cenacle. The liturgy moves through the city on foot, station by station, and each text is read on the ground where the text happened.
suggested_refs: The church on Sion predating the medieval Cenacle
sources: Egeria, Itinerarium ch. 27 and 43, trans. McClure and Feltoe (CCEL)

segments.name: The Jordan and the Land Beyond

stops.name: The Jordan, where the tribes crossed dry
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed. The excursion is undated in the text and placed here between the Easter and September observances she records.
stops.campa: Guides show her the place on the Jordan where Israel crossed on dry ground under Joshua, and upstream the altar Reuben, Gad and the half tribe of Manasseh are said to have raised on the eastern bank. Later Byzantine tradition will fix the baptism of Christ on this same stretch of water, the reach now called Qasr al-Yahud. Egeria's reason for stopping is the older story. She has come for the crossing of the tribes, and the Gospel scene is not what her hosts point at.
suggested_refs: The Qasr al-Yahud reach of the lower Jordan
sources: Egeria, Itinerarium ch. 10, trans. McClure and Feltoe (CCEL)

stops.name: Livias, foundations still visible to this day
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; undated in the text.
stops.campa: At Livias in the Jordan plain she is shown the ground where Israel camped before entering the promised land, its foundations, she writes, still visible to this day. Herod Antipas renamed the town for the empress Livia, and the plain around it carries a whole cluster of Exodus sites within a morning's ride. From here a detour of six miles brings her to the spring her guides identify as the rock Moses struck. The wilderness has an itinerary now, and priests to conduct it.
suggested_refs: Tell er-Rameh, the site generally identified with Livias
sources: Egeria, Itinerarium ch. 10 and 12, trans. McClure and Feltoe (CCEL)

stops.name: Mount Nebo, the view named as proof
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; undated in the text.
stops.campa: She rides most of the way up Nebo by donkey and finishes on foot at the small church on the summit, where monks show her the place holy Moses died. From the height she sees the Dead Sea, Livias, Jericho, the whole span of Palestine, and names Esebon, Sasdra and Fogor in the distance. They point out Segor, the only one of the five cities of the plain still standing. The pillar of Lot's wife, she is told, cannot be seen: the water has covered it, and only the place is shown.
stops.quote: the pillar itself cannot be seen, only the place is shown, the pillar is said to have been covered by the Dead Sea
stops.quote_source: Egeria, Itinerarium ch. 12, trans. McClure and Feltoe, The Pilgrimage of Etheria (1919)
suggested_refs: The summit church at Siyagha, Mount Nebo, and the sanctuary of Agios Lot at Deir 'Ain 'Abata
sources: Egeria, Itinerarium ch. 11-12, trans. McClure and Feltoe (CCEL)

stops.name: Sedima, the city they call Salem
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed. The northern excursion is undated; it is placed before the September dedication feast on sequence alone.
stops.campa: On the bank of the Jordan she is guided to Sedima, which her hosts identify as Salem, the city of Melchizedek, king and priest who blessed Abraham. A church stands on the hill over foundations pointed out as the king's own house. The identification rests on the memory of the villagers who tell it to her, and she says so; no inscription and no record confirms it, then or since. Melchizedek occupies three verses of Genesis, and here he has a hill, a set of foundations and a church.
suggested_refs: Salim, near Nablus, the village Egeria's guides equated with Melchizedek's Salem
sources: Egeria, Itinerarium ch. 13-14, trans. McClure and Feltoe (CCEL)

stops.name: Aenon near Salim, the pool still in use
stops.date_confidence: same day as the previous stop by her own account: the site lies two hundred paces off. Undated in the text.
stops.campa: Two hundred paces from Sedima lies Aenon, the spring where John baptized because water was plentiful there. Egeria finds a pool fed by the spring and a garden called Saint John's, and is told that baptisms are still performed in it at Easter. A Gospel place name unattested anywhere outside the text has survived here as working practice rather than as a monument. Easter after Easter the water is used, and that use is the whole of the evidence that this is the place.
suggested_refs: The spring and pool of Aenon, in continuous baptismal use in the 380s
sources: Egeria, Itinerarium ch. 15, trans. McClure and Feltoe (CCEL)

stops.name: Thesbe, the cave where the holy man sat
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; undated in the text.
stops.campa: Her guides show her Thesbe, the city scripture gives as the birthplace of Elijah, with the cave where the holy man sat and the tomb of one Getha beside it. The stop belongs to a run of prophet sites strung along the road east, each resting on local report. Modern scholarship places ancient Thesbe near Listib in the hills of northern Jordan, tentatively, beside the mound that Arabic still calls Mar Elias. No inscription names the place, then or now. The cave is shown to her, and what is shown is all there is.
suggested_refs: Listib and Tell Mar Elias in Ajloun, the tentative site of Tishbe
sources: Egeria, Itinerarium ch. 16, trans. McClure and Feltoe (CCEL)

stops.name: Carneas, the tomb of Job under a church half built
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; undated in the text.
stops.campa: At Carneas, formerly called Dennaba, in the land of Ausitis, she is shown the tomb of Job in a cave beneath a church still going up, begun by a Roman officer she calls the tribune. The site is generally identified with al-Shaykh Saad in the Hauran. A colossal Egyptian statue of the Old Kingdom stands in that village, and later folklore will read it as an image of Job himself. Egeria sees the half built church and the cave under it and writes the name she is given.
stops.quote: The city of Job is now called Carneas, but it was formerly called Dennaba, in the land of Ausitis.
stops.quote_source: Egeria, Itinerarium ch. 16, trans. McClure and Feltoe, The Pilgrimage of Etheria (1919)
suggested_refs: Al-Shaykh Saad in the Hauran, historically Karnaim and Dair Ayyub
sources: Egeria, Itinerarium ch. 16, trans. McClure and Feltoe (CCEL)

segments.name: The Year of the Holy City

stops.name: Golgotha, the dies enceniarum
stops.date_confidence: the feast is fixed in September by her account; the day and year are reconstructed.
stops.campa: In September the city keeps the dies enceniarum, the eight day feast commemorating the consecration of the churches Constantine raised on Golgotha, and Egeria sets its splendour beside Easter and Epiphany. Nine centuries later Maimonides will pray on the platform above the ruined Temple in this same city, and Ibn Battuta will log Jerusalem as the third sanctuary in passing. She is one traveller in a long line of them, and the earliest whose written account of the walking survives.
suggested_refs: The September dedication feast of the Constantinian churches on Golgotha
sources: Egeria, Itinerarium, liturgical calendar section
Encyclopedia.com, 'Egeria, Itinerarium of'
maimonides.journey.json
ibn_battuta.journey.json

stops.name: Bethlehem, the vigil that opens the octave
stops.date_confidence: the vigil is fixed to the eve of Epiphany by her account; the year is reconstructed within the Devos frame.
stops.campa: An all night vigil at Bethlehem opens the eight days of Epiphany, kept at the shepherds' field and at the cave church over the birthplace. Monks relay the prayer in shifts so that the praise does not stop across the octave. The basilica standing over the grotto was consecrated in 339, forty four years before she kneels in it. She gives the order of psalms and readings assigned to each night of the octave, which is why the feast can be reconstructed at all.
suggested_refs: The Constantinian Church of the Nativity, consecrated 31 May 339
sources: Egeria, Itinerarium ch. 25, trans. McClure and Feltoe (CCEL)

stops.name: The Eleona, fourth day of the octave
stops.date_confidence: the day within the octave is Egeria's; the year is reconstructed.
stops.campa: On the fourth day of the octave the community climbs to the Eleona, the church on the Mount of Olives built over the cave where Christ taught the disciples, raised, tradition holds, by Constantine's mother. The name is Greek for olive grove and marks the ground rather than any relic held in it. From here Jerusalem's feast moves outward across the hills that ring the city. The Gospels put the teaching on the mount and name no cave; Jerusalem has found one and built over it.
suggested_refs: The Eleona basilica on the Mount of Olives
sources: Egeria, Itinerarium ch. 25-26, trans. McClure and Feltoe (CCEL)

stops.name: The Lazarium at Bethany, fifth day of the octave
stops.date_confidence: the day within the octave is Egeria's; the year is reconstructed.
stops.campa: On the fifth day they process to the Lazarium at Bethany, fifteen hundred paces from the city by her count, built over the tomb from which Lazarus was called out. A single Gospel scene has become an annual station that any pilgrim in Jerusalem can walk to before noon. Egeria gives the distance in paces and the day in the octave, and adds nothing to either. She is writing for sisters at home who will never make the walk, and the paces are for them.
suggested_refs: The Lazarium church at Bethany, station of the Epiphany octave
sources: Egeria, Itinerarium ch. 29, trans. McClure and Feltoe (CCEL)

stops.name: The Mount of Olives, the procession with branches
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed. Easter 384 fell on 24 March by the Julian reckoning, putting Palm Sunday on 17 March; Egeria names the day of the week, not the date.
stops.campa: At the seventh hour the whole city goes up to the Mount of Olives, and in the late afternoon the people walk back down into Jerusalem in procession, carrying branches and singing. Jesus rode this same slope in the atlas three and a half centuries earlier. Egeria's description of the Palm Sunday procession is the earliest eyewitness account of the observance anywhere, and every later reconstruction of it goes back to the letter she was writing for her sisters at home.
suggested_refs: The Palm Sunday descent from the Mount of Olives, earliest attested in Egeria
sources: Egeria, Itinerarium, Holy Week section
Wikipedia, 'Itinerarium Egeriae'
jesus.journey.json

stops.name: Golgotha, the wood of the Cross brought out
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed. Good Friday of 384 falls on 22 March if Easter fell on 24 March; Egeria names the day of the week only.
stops.campa: On the Friday the bishop is seated at Golgotha behind the Cross, the relic of the True Cross is brought out, and the people come forward one at a time to venerate the wood. Constantine's builders uncovered this rock and this tomb some sixty years before she stands here. Her account of the ceremony is the earliest surviving eyewitness description of it anywhere, and the later reconstructions of Holy Week are built on her paragraphs because there is nothing older to build on.
suggested_refs: The Good Friday veneration of the True Cross at Golgotha
sources: Egeria, Itinerarium, Holy Week section
Encyclopedia.com, 'Egeria, Itinerarium of'
constantino_el_grande.journey.json

stops.name: Antioch, a week and no relic
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed backwards from Devos's dating of her arrival at Edessa in April 384; Egeria gives a stay of one week and no date.
stops.campa: After Easter she turns north, and at Antioch she halts a full week. The great Syrian city gets no relic and no legend in her text, only the pause: rest before the harder road east. Around her the largest Christian population in the empire is split into rival congregations, each with its own bishop, in the fiercest doctrinal quarrel of the century. She does not mention it. What interests her is the road, and past the road the Euphrates, and past the Euphrates a country she has no obligation to reach.
suggested_refs: Antioch on the Orontes, hinge of the road from Palestine into Mesopotamia
sources: Egeria, Itinerarium ch. 17, trans. McClure and Feltoe (CCEL)

stops.name: Hierapolis, the metropolis without its goddess
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed from the Devos chronology; undated in the text.
stops.campa: She calls Hierapolis, in the province she names Augustofratensis, a beautiful and wealthy city and the metropolis of the region, and notes that the Euphrates crossing lies fifteen miles further on. The place is Manbij, which for centuries housed the temple of the Syrian goddess Atargatis that Lucian described at length. Egeria says nothing of it. A Christian itinerary can pass through a famous pagan sanctuary and record only the mileage to the next river.
suggested_refs: Manbij, ancient Hierapolis Bambyce, seat of the cult of Atargatis
sources: Egeria, Itinerarium ch. 18, trans. McClure and Feltoe (CCEL)

stops.name: The Euphrates, huge and terrible
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed. The crossing point is approximate: Egeria gives its distance from Hierapolis, fifteen miles, and names no ferry.
stops.campa: Fifteen miles beyond Hierapolis she reaches the Euphrates and calls it huge and terrible, its current running down like the Rhone, though far larger. No bridge spans it here, and the party crosses in large ships. That comparison to the Rhone is the sentence Karl Meister will use in 1909 to argue she came from Gaul, and one reason her homeland is contested still. On the far bank Mesopotamia begins, and with it the leg of the journey nobody at home asked her to make.
suggested_refs: The Euphrates ferry crossing fifteen miles east of Hierapolis
sources: Egeria, Itinerarium ch. 18, trans. McClure and Feltoe (CCEL)
Karl Meister (1909)

stops.name: Edessa, the memorial of Thomas and the letter of Abgar
stops.date_confidence: April 384 by Devos's reconstruction of the chronology; the day is not given in the text.
stops.campa: Twenty five stations out from Jerusalem she reaches Edessa and goes straight to the memorial of the apostle Thomas, where his body lies entire, in a church she calls very great and very beautiful. The bishop receives her, a man she describes as truly devout, both monk and confessor. He shows her the palace of King Abgar and a marble statue that shines like pearl, and tells her how the letter of Christ once turned a Persian siege. She stays three days and reads aloud from a book of Thomas.
stops.quote: Departing thence, we arrived at Edessa in the Name of Christ our God, and, on our arrival, we straightway repaired to the church and memorial of saint Thomas.
stops.quote_source: Egeria, Itinerarium, trans. McClure and Feltoe, The Pilgrimage of Etheria (1919), p. 32
suggested_refs: The shrine of Thomas at Edessa; the Abgar correspondence as Egeria saw it displayed
sources: Egeria, Itinerarium ch. 19, trans. McClure and Feltoe (1919), pp. 30-32
Paul Devos, 'Egerie a Edesse', Analecta Bollandiana 85 (1967)
Oxford Cult of Saints database E05223

stops.name: Harran, the well and the feast of Helpidius
stops.date_confidence: the feast day, 23 April, is Egeria's own; the year follows Devos.
stops.campa: At Harran the bishop takes her to the house of Abraham, its foundations built into a church, and to the well whence holy Rebecca used to fetch water. She finds scarcely a single Christian in the city: the monks and ascetics of the region come in only for Easter and for the feast of the martyr Helpidius on the twenty third of April, which by good fortune falls while she is there. A mile off she is shown the memorials of Nahor and of Bethuel, Abraham's brother and his great nephew.
stops.quote: he deigned to take us to the well whence holy Rebecca used to fetch water
stops.quote_source: Egeria, Itinerarium ch. 20, trans. McClure and Feltoe, The Pilgrimage of Etheria (1919)
suggested_refs: Harran, ancient Carrhae, and the church built into the house of Abraham
sources: Egeria, Itinerarium ch. 20, trans. McClure and Feltoe (CCEL)

stops.name: Fadana, the stone Jacob rolled
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed from the sequence; Egeria gives the distance from Harran, six miles, and no date.
stops.campa: Six miles from Harran she is brought to the well where Jacob watered Rachel's flocks, marked by the great stone he is said to have rolled from its mouth and by a large and beautiful church. Nearby stands Fadana, identified as Laban's farm, with Laban's memorial and the spot where Rachel is said to have taken her father's household gods. Genesis is being walked verse by verse here, each stop a sentence of scripture with a building on it and a guide who knows the sentence.
suggested_refs: The well of Jacob near Harran and the village of Fadana, Laban's farm
sources: Egeria, Itinerarium ch. 20, trans. McClure and Feltoe (CCEL)

segments.name: The Road Home, and the Torn Page

stops.name: Tarsus, seen for the second time
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the return leg is undated throughout.
stops.campa: On the road home she passes back through Tarsus, metropolis of Cilicia and birthplace of Paul, a city she had already seen on the outward journey years before. She gives it a name and a line. The outward road itself is gone: the manuscript's missing opening carried it, and every place she reached before Sinai survives only in remarks like this one, dropped in passing while she crosses country she is looking at for the second time. Half her pilgrimage is legible only in the shrugs of the half that survived.
suggested_refs: Tarsus in Cilicia, a stop on both the outward and the return legs
sources: Egeria, Itinerarium ch. 22-23, trans. McClure and Feltoe (CCEL)

stops.name: Hagia Thekla, the deaconess Marthana
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; Egeria gives a stay of two days and no date.
stops.campa: Fifteen hundred paces outside Seleucia in Isauria stands the shrine of Thecla, a walled enclosure holding nothing but the countless cells of monks and nuns around the church. The deaconess Marthana governs the cells of the virgins there, an old friend from Jerusalem, and Egeria's greeting of her is unguarded. She stays two days. It is one of the few stops in the surviving text where the reason for turning aside is a person and not a place in scripture.
suggested_refs: The Hagia Thekla enclosure at Meryemlik, outside Silifke
sources: Egeria, Itinerarium ch. 23, trans. McClure and Feltoe (CCEL)

stops.name: Chalcedon, the martyrium of Euphemia
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed. Egeria gives no length of stay at all: the next sentence has her crossing the water on another day, implying a single night.
stops.campa: She arrives at Chalcedon and stops for the martyrium of Euphemia, killed there under Diocletian some eighty years earlier and already well known to her from an earlier visit. She names no length of stay; the following sentence has her crossing the water on another day. Sixty seven years after she prays here, the bishops of the empire will meet in this church and divide the eastern Christian world over two natures in one person. What she sees is a martyr's tomb with the capital in view across the strait.
stops.quote: I arrived at Chalcedon, where I stopped on account of the famous martyr-memorial of S. Eufimia already well known to me from a former visit
stops.quote_source: Egeria, Itinerarium ch. 23, trans. McClure and Feltoe, The Pilgrimage of Etheria (1919)
suggested_refs: The martyrium of Euphemia at Chalcedon, later site of the 451 council
sources: Egeria, Itinerarium ch. 23, trans. McClure and Feltoe (CCEL)

stops.name: Constantinople, the text breaks off
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed. This is the last place the surviving text names; nothing dates it, and nothing after it survives.
stops.campa: In Constantinople she visits the Church of the Apostles and the memorials of many other martyrs, and writes to her sisters that she means to go on to Ephesus, to the shrine of Saint John. Then the text stops. Whether she reached Ephesus, whether she went home, when she died and where: none of it is known, because the last leaves of the only surviving copy are gone. The journey does not end in the record. It is cut off in the middle of a stated intention.
suggested_refs: The Church of the Holy Apostles at Constantinople, last site named in the surviving text
sources: Egeria, Itinerarium ch. 23, trans. McClure and Feltoe (CCEL)
Wikipedia, 'Itinerarium Egeriae'

segments.name: The Codex, and the Name Restored

stops.name: El Bierzo, Valerius names her
stops.date_confidence: c. 680, following the dating of Valerius of Bierzo (c. 630-695) and his work with Abbot Donadeus; a widely repeated 'mid-7th century' or 650 is roughly a generation early.
stops.campa: Near Astorga, three centuries after she stopped writing, a monk named Valerius composes a letter to the brothers of the Bierzo praising a woman he calls Egeria, sprung from the farthest shore of the western sea, who went to the ends of the earth. He calls her a nun. Hagith Sivan argues in 1988 that he may be wrong, since devout laywomen of that age were addressed as sisters too and the diary claims no vows for itself. His letter is the only external witness to her name.
stops.quote: sprung from the farthest shore of the western sea, the Ocean
stops.quote_source: Valerius of Bierzo, Epistola ad fratres, as translated in McClure and Feltoe, The Pilgrimage of Etheria (1919), p. viii
suggested_refs: The Vita vel epistola beatissimae Egeriae of Valerius of Bierzo
sources: Valerius of Bierzo, Epistola ad fratres, ed. Diaz y Diaz in Maraval, SC 296 (1982)
Hagith Sivan, 'Who Was Egeria?', HTR 81 (1988)
Encyclopedia.com, 'Valerio of Bierzo'

stops.name: Monte Cassino, the single hand
stops.date_confidence: 11th century; the year 1050 is a placeholder within that century, and no colophon dates the copy.
stops.campa: On the mountain of Monte Cassino, in the eleventh century, a scribe copies her diary into a codex alongside the hymns and the treatise on the Mysteries of Hilary of Poitiers. He is copying from something already damaged: the opening leaves are gone and so is the end, and the author's name went with them. Every word of Egeria that anyone has read since descends from this one hand. A ninth century fragment identified by Jesus Alturo in 2005 is the only independent witness to any of it.
suggested_refs: Codex Aretinus 405, folios 31-74, copied at Monte Cassino
sources: Encyclopedia.com, 'Egeria, Itinerarium of'
Wikipedia, 'Itinerarium Egeriae'
Jesus Alturo (2005)

stops.name: Arezzo, the wrong name and then the right one
stops.date_confidence: the discovery year 1884 is attested; the month and day are not recorded and default to 01-01.
stops.campa: In 1884 Gian Francesco Gamurrini finds the codex in the library of the Confraternity of Santa Maria dei Laici at Arezzo. He publishes it in 1887 as S. Silviae Aquitanae peregrinatio ad loca sancta, attributing it to Silvia of Aquitaine, sister of the prefect Rufinus, a different fourth century noblewoman entirely. In 1903 Marius Ferotin reads Valerius against the text and puts the right name on it. Fifteen centuries anonymous, then sixteen years misattributed.
stops.quote: This book was discovered by Signor Gamurrini in a MS. of the eleventh century at Arezzo, and he published it first in 1887 and again, in a correcter edition, in 1888.
stops.quote_source: Translators' Introduction, McClure and Feltoe, The Pilgrimage of Etheria (1919), p. vii
suggested_refs: Codex Aretinus 405, Biblioteca della Fraternita dei Laici, Arezzo
sources: Wikipedia, 'Itinerarium Egeriae'
Encyclopedia.com, 'Egeria, Itinerarium of'
McClure and Feltoe (1919), Introduction, pp. vii-viii

stops.name: Santiago de Compostela, a statue at the crossroads
stops.date_confidence: November 2022 per the regional press; the exact day of the installation is not recorded in the reachable reporting.
stops.campa: In November 2022 a sculpture of Egeria is set up at the remodelled Concheiros crossroads, on the last stretch of road into Santiago, honouring her as the first documented woman pilgrim. Galicia calls her the first Galician pilgrim. The claim rests on Ferotin's reading of one clause in Valerius, contested by Meister's philology since 1909, and her own road never came within two thousand miles of this city. The statue stands anyway, at the end of a pilgrim route she helped invent.
suggested_refs: The Egeria sculpture at the Concheiros crossroads, Santiago de Compostela, November 2022
sources: La Voz de Galicia, November 2022
El Progreso / Diario de Pontevedra, 'Egeria, la primera peregrina gallega' (2019)
